publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: In order to elucidate the origin of galactic ridge X-ray emission, we analyzed Suzaku data taken at various regions along the galactic plane, and studied their Fe-K emission line features. Suzaku resolved the Fe line complex into three narrow lines at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex> 6.4 keV, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex> 6.7 keV and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex> 6.97 keV, which are K-lines from neutral (or low-ionized), He-like, and H-like iron respectively. The 6.7 keV line is clearly seen in all of the observed regions, and its longitudinal distribution is consistent with that determined from previous observations. The 6.4 keV emission line was also found in various galactic plane regions (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$b\sim0^{\circ}$</tex>). Differences in the flux ratios of the 6.4 keV/6.7 keV and 6.97 keV/6.7 keV lines between the galactic plane and the galactic center regions were studied and its implication was discussed.

articleTitle: Relativistic Spectra of Hot Black-Hole Winds
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We examine hybrid thermal-nonthermal synchrotron spectra from a spherically symmetric, optically-thin wind, taking into account the relativistic effect. In relativistic flow from the central object, due to the relativistic beaming effect, the observed spectra often shift towards high frequency and high intensity directions. In optically thin outflows, however, we find that the intensity of the observed spectra decreases compared with that of the emitted ones, although the peak frequency shifts towards the high-frequency direction. This is because in the optically thin outflows we can see the far-side flows that go away from the observer. We thus carefully consider optically thin relativistic flows around a black hole, such as Sgr A<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^\ast$</tex>.

articleTitle: Suzaku Observation Adjacent to the South End of the Radio Arc
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Suzaku observed the Galactic center region near the Radio Arc at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>20<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^\prime$</tex>; southeast of Sagittarius A<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">*</sup>. In an 18<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^\prime$</tex> × 18<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^\prime$</tex> field of view, we found four distinct X-ray sources: a bright star and a diffuse source associated with star clusters in the soft band (0.5–2.0 keV), a small clump in a higher energy band (4–6 keV), and a peculiar clump in the 6.4 keV line band. The latter two clumps are located at the south end of the Radio Arc. This paper reports on the results, and discusses the origin of these X-ray sources, with a particular emphasis on small clumps.

articleTitle: A Time-Series Analysis of the H$\alpha$ Emission Line in V3885 Sagitarii
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Flickering is a phenomenon related to mass accretion observed among many classes of astrophysical objects. In this paper we present a study of flickering emission lines and the continuum of the cataclysmic variable V3885 Sgr. The flickering behavior was first analyzed through statistical analysis and the power spectra of lightcurves. Autocorrelation techniques were then employed to estimate the flickering timescale of flares. A cross-correlation study between the line and its underlying continuum variability is presented. The cross-correlation between the photometric and spectroscopic data is also discussed. Periodograms, calculated using emission-line data, show a behavior that is similar to those obtained from photometric datasets found in the literature, with a plateau at lower frequencies and a power-law at higher frequencies. The power-law index is consistent with stochastic events. The cross-correlation study indicates the presence of a correlation between the variability on H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex> and its underlying continuum. Flickering timescales derived from the photometric data were estimated to be 25 min for two lightcurves and 10 min for one of them. The average timescales of the line flickering is 40 min, while for its underlying continuum it drops to 20 min.

articleTitle: Observational Appearance of Black Hole Winds
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We examine the observational appearance of an optically thick, spherically symmetric, relativistic wind (a black hole wind). In a relativistic flow, the apparent optical depth becomes small in the downstream direction, while it is large in the upstream direction due to the relativistic effect. Hence, the apparent photosphere of the relativistic flow depends on the flow velocity and direction as well as the density distribution. We calculated the temperature distribution of the apparent photosphere of the optically thick black hole wind, where the wind speed was assumed to be constant and radiation dominates matter, for various values of the wind speed and mass-outflow rate. We found that the limb-darkening effect is strongly enhanced in the relativistic regime. We also found that the observed luminosities of the black hole wind become large as the wind speed increases, but do not depend on the mass-outflow rate.

articleTitle: Advection-Dominated Accretion Disks: Geometrically Slim or Thick?
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We revisit the vertical structure of black-hole accretion disks in spherical coordinates. By comparing the advective cooling with the viscous heating, we show that advection-dominated disks are geometrically thick, i.e., with a half-opening angle of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Delta\theta$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$>$</tex> 2<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pi/$</tex>5, rather than being slim, as supposed previously in the literature.

articleTitle: Period Change and Possible Magnetic Braking in WY Cancri
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: In this paper, the orbital period change of the RS CVn-type binary system WY Cnc is analyzed through a detailed description of the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$O-C$</tex> curve by a weighted least-squares method. It is found that the period variation is suffering a secular period decrease at a rate of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$dp/dt$</tex>=-1.20 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-7}$</tex>dy<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>. Since WY Cnc is a typical detached binary system, and both components are late-type stars, the long-term period decrease may be caused by angular momentum loss via magnetic braking.

articleTitle: Suzaku Observations of SGR1900+14 and SGR1806-20
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Spectral and timing studies of Suzaku ToO observations of two SGRs, 1900+14 and 1806-20, are presented. The X-ray quiescent emission spectra were well fitted by a two blackbody function, or a blackbody plus a power-law model. The non-thermal hard component discovered by INTEGRAL was detected by PIN diodes and its spectrum was reproduced by the power-law model reported by INTEGRAL. The XIS detected a periodicity of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$P$</tex>= 5.1998<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex>0.0002 s for SGR1900+14 and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$P$</tex>= 7.6022<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex>0.0007 s for SGR 1806-20. The pulsed fraction was related to the burst activity for SGR 1900+14.

articleTitle: Anti-Correlation of Near-Infrared and X-Ray Variations of the Microquasar GRS 1915+105 in the Soft State
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present detailed, long term near-infrared (NIR) light curves of GRS 1915+105 obtained in 2007–2008, covering its long “soft state” for the first time. From our NIR monitoring and X-ray data of the All Sky Monitor onboard Rossi X-ray Timing Explorer, we discovered that the NIR flux dropped by <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$>$</tex> 1 mag during short X-ray flares with a time-scale of days. Upon termination of the soft state, the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$H-K_{\rm s}$</tex> color reddened and the anti-correlation pattern was broken. The observed <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$H-K_{\rm s}$</tex> color variation suggests that the dominant NIR source was an accretion disk during the soft state. The short X-ray flares during the soft state were associated with spectral hardening in X-rays and increasing radio emission, indicating jet ejection. The temporal NIR fading during the X-ray flares thus implies a sudden decrease in the contribution of the accretion disk when a jet is ejected.

articleTitle: Frequency Separation Variations of the Solar Low-Degree p-Modes
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Variations of frequency separations of low-degree p-modes have been studied over the solar-activity cycle. The studied separations were obtained from the frequencies of low-degree p-modes of the Global Oscillation Network Group (GONG). The 10.7 cm radio flux was used as an index of solar activity. Small separations of the p-mode frequencies are considered to be mainly dependent on the conditions in stellar interiors. Thus, they could be applied to a diagnosis of the changes in the stellar interior. Our calculation results show that the magnitudes of the variations of the mean large separations are less than 1<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sigma$</tex> over the solar-activity cycle. Small separations show different behaviors in the ascending and descending phases of activity. In the ascending phase, variations of the small separations are less than 1<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sigma$</tex>. However, the small separations had systematic shifts during the period from 2004 to 2007. These shifts were roughly 1<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sigma$</tex> or more. The variations in the ratios of the small-to-large separations with time were similar to the changes of the small separations. The effects of the changes in the large separations on the ratios were negligible. The variations of the separations may be a consequence of influence from the surface activity, or systematic errors in measurements, or some processes taking place in the solar interior.

articleTitle: Multiwavelength Photon Spectra from Microquasars
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We have studied multiwavelength photon emission from microquasars based on the framework of a leptonic jet model. In this model, non-thermal photons are produced by synchrotron, relativistic Bremsstrahlung, and angular dependent inverse Compton processes; they suffer a periodic orbital modulation due to the effects of different accretion rates and a variation of the soft photon density at different orbital phases as well as the orbital-phase and angular dependence <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\gamma$</tex>–<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\gamma$</tex> absorption and IC scattering. We applied this model to two possible microquasars, LS 5039 and LS I +61 303, and our results can roughly reproduce their observed spectral properties and the variability of these sources.

articleTitle: Beam Pattern Measurements and Observational Evaluations of the ALMA/ACA 12-m Antenna
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We have evaluated the beam pattern of the ALMA/ACA 12-m antenna with total power observations of Jupiter and the Moon. Models of the expected beam pattern as it passes across Jupiter and the Moon were derived in consideration of the radiation pattern of the actual receiving system and the surface error of the main reflector. Since the profiles of the measured beam patterns were consistent with those of the models within the range from the peak to -20 dB, we confirmed that the antenna achieved the beam pattern expected from its optical design. After this confirmation, we performed astronomical observations. In addition to the detection of the CS <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J$</tex>= 3–2 (146.969026 GHz) spectrum toward Orion KL, the change in the Moon intensity was successfully detected during the total lunar eclipse during 2008 February 20–21. A time lag longer than 10 min in the millimeter-wave eclipse relative to the corresponding optical eclipse ephemeris was detected. Mapping observations of the Sun revealed the structure of the chromospheric networks at 147 GHz. These astronomical observations confirmed that the ACA 12-m antenna could be successfully operated under various operating conditions.

articleTitle: High-Resolution Spectroscopy of T Tauri Stars
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We have conducted high-resolution spectroscopic observations of a sample of both classical and weak-line T Tauri stars embedded in the Taurus-Auriga molecular cloud using the Okayama Astrophysical Observatory’s 188 cm telescope equipped with HIDES (HIgh Dispersion Echelle Spectrograph). Utilizing the ratios of equivalent widths of specific lines, we efficiently eliminated the effects of “veiling” and determined the atmospheric parameters individually for each object. Eight pairs of temperature-sensitive line-ratios were selected to derive the effective temperature with high precision and reliability. As for the surface gravity, we have developed a new method to determine the value. The method was first tested on observed spectral standards, and the derived surface gravities had a less than 5% deviation from the values in the literature. The derived surface gravities are well within the range of the assumed values for T Tauri stars.

articleTitle: Period Changes of DF Hydrae: Evidence of Mass Transfer and the Presence of a Cool Tertiary Companion
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Combining our six new determined times of light minimum obtained from 2001 to 2007 with others compiled from the literature, we investigated the period changes of DF Hydrae. The general trend of the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$O-C$</tex> curve based on all available data reveals that the period of the binary star is increasing continuously at a rate of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$dP/dt$</tex>=+1.11(<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex>0.02) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-7}$</tex>dyr<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>. After the long-term period increase was removed from the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$O-C$</tex> diagram, it was discovered that the residuals of the CCD and photoelectric observations suggest a small-amplitude cyclic oscillation with a period of 21.5 years. The continuous period increase can be explained by mass transfer from the secondary to the primary, indicating that DF Hydrae is on the TRO-controlled stage of the evolutionary scenario proposed by Qian. The cyclic period variation suggests that DF Hydrae is a triple system containing a cool tertiary component with a mass of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_3$</tex>sin<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${i^{\prime}}$</tex>= 0.21<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_{\odot}$</tex> in a 21.5-year orbit. By removing angular momentum from the central binary system via Kozai oscillation or a combination of the Kozai cycle and tidal friction, the tertiary companion may play an important role for the formation and evolution of the contact system, which makes the eclipsing pair to have a short initial orbital period (i.e., <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$P$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$<$</tex> 5<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\rm d}$</tex>). In that case, the detached progenitor of DF Hydrae evolves into the present contact configuration via a combination of magnetic braking and a case A mass transfer.

articleTitle: Discoveries of 3 K-Shell Lines of Iron and a Coherent Pulsation of 593 s from SAX J1748.2-2808
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: SAX J1748.2-2808 is a unique X-ray object with a flat spectrum and strong emission lines at 6.4–7.0 keV. The Suzaku satellite resolved the emission lines into 3 K-shell lines from neutral and highly ionized irons. A clear coherent pulsation with a period of 593 s was found from the Suzaku and XMM-Newton archives. These facts favor that SAX J1748.2-2808 is an intermediate polar, a subclass of a magnetized white dwarf binary (cataclysmic variable). This paper reports on details of the findings, and discusses the origin of this source.

articleTitle: Search for Sc-K Line Emission from RX J0852.0-4622 Supernova Remnant with Suzaku
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We searched for evidence of line emission around 4 keV from the northwestern rim of the supernova remnant RX J0852.0-4622 using Suzaku XIS data. Several papers have reported on the detection of an emission line around 4.1 keV from this region of the sky. This line would arise from <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$K$</tex>-band fluorescence by <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{44}$</tex>Sc, the immediate decay product of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{44}$</tex>Ti. We performed spectral analysis for the entire portion of the NW rim of the remnant within the XIS field of view, as well as various regions corresponding to regions of published claims of line emission. We found no line emission around 4.1 keV anywhere, and are able to set a restrictive upper limit to the X-ray flux: 1.1 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-6}$</tex>s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-2}$</tex> for the entire field. For every region, our flux upper limit falls below that of the previously claimed detection. Therefore, we conclude that, to date, no definite X-ray line feature from Sc-K emission has been detected in the NW rim of RX J0852.0-4622. Our negative-detection supports the recent claim that RX J0852-4622 is neither young (1700–4000 yr) nor nearby (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>750 pc).

articleTitle: A Search for Molecular Gas toward a BzK-Selected Star-Forming Galaxy at z = 2.044
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present a search for CO (3–2) emission in SDF-26821, a <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$BzK$</tex>-selected star-forming galaxy (sBzK) at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z$</tex>= 2.044, using the 45-m telescope of the Nobeyama Radio Observatory and the Nobeyama Millimeter Array. We did not detect significant emission, and derived the 2<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sigma$</tex> limits: CO luminosity of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L^\prime_{\rm {CO}}$</tex> 3.1 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{10}$</tex>Kkms<tex xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L_{\rm {FIR}}/L^\prime_{\rm {CO}}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$>$</tex> 57 xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{2}$</tex>)<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>, and molecular gas mass of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_{\rm {H_2}}$</tex> 2.5 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{10}$</tex>, assuming a velocity width of 200 kms<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex> and a CO-to-H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_2$</tex> conversion factor of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha_{\rm {CO}}$</tex>=<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$0.8$</tex> (Kkms<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>pc<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{2}$</tex>)<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>. The ratio <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L_{\rm {FIR}}/L^\prime_{\rm {CO}}$</tex>, a measure of the star-formation efficiency (SFE), is comparable to, or higher than, the two <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex> 1.5 sBzKs detected in CO (2-1) previously, suggesting that sBzKs can have a wide range of SFEs. Comparisons of far-infrared luminosity, gas mass, and stellar mass among the sBzKs suggest that SDF-26821 is at an earlier stage of forming stars with a similar SFE and/or more efficiently forming stars than the two <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex> 1.5 sBzKs. The higher SFEs and specific star-formation rates of the sBzKs compared to local spirals are indicative of a difference in the star-formation modes between these systems, suggesting that sBzKs are not just scaled-up versions of local spirals.

articleTitle: On Period Variations of the K-Type Eclipsing Binary BM Ursae Majoris
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: From new CCD observations, 11 light minimum times are presented in this paper. The orbital period change of a W UMa-type eclipsing binary, BM Urase Majoris, was investigated, based on all available times of light minimum. It was discovered that the orbital period of the binary shows cyclic oscillation, superimposed on a secular period decrease. The amplitude and the period of the cyclic variation are <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$A$</tex>= 0.0101(<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex>0.0004)d and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$P_{3}$</tex>= 30.8(<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex>0.2)yr, respectively. This kind of cyclic variation may be due to a light-time effect via an unseen third body. If the existence of an additional body is true, it may remove a great amount of angular momentum from the central system, and may play an important role in the formation of close binary. The orbital period continuously decreases at a rate of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$dP/dt$</tex>=-7.49(<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex>0.16) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-8}$</tex>dyr<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>, which may be due to mass transfer from the primary to the secondary, accompanying mass and angular-momentum loss from the binary system. The orbital period decrease, accompanying mass and angular momentum loss, would cause the contact degree to increase. Therefore, this binary will evolve into a deep contact configuration.

articleTitle: An Orbital Period Investigation of the Solar-Type Overcontact Binary V700 Cygni
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Orbital period changes of the solar-type contact binary V700 Cyg were investigated based on one new eclipse time combined with the others collected from the literature. A cyclic oscillation, with a period of 39.1 yr and an amplitude of 0.<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\rm d}$</tex>0197, was found to be superimposed on a secular period increase at a rate of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$dP/dt$</tex>=+2.8 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-8}{\rm d}$</tex> yr<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>. Weak evidence indicates that there exists another small-amplitude period oscillation. The long-term period increase is in agreement with the conclusion that high-mass ratio W-type overcontact binaries usually show period increasing. This suggests that it may be in the stage controlled by thermal relaxation oscillations. Cyclic period oscillation can be explained as being the result of a light-travel time effect via the presence of an additional body. On the other hand, since both components of V700 Cyg are late-type stars, the period oscillation may be evidence of magnetic activity cycles of the two component stars.

articleTitle: New Period Investigation of Algol-like Near-Contact Binary EG Cephei
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The Algol-like Near Contact Binary EG Cephei was observed in 2008 October. One new observed time of the secondary minimum was derived in <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$BV(IR)_{\rm c}$</tex> bands. It turns out that the times of minima at longer wavelengths occur earlier than the shorter ones. All of the available eclipse times, including 735 epochs, spanning more than 100 years were analyzed. A period oscillation with a period of 35.8(<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex>0.1)yr and an amplitude of about 0.0037(<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex>0.0002)d was found, while undergoing a secular increase at a rate of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$dP/dt$</tex>= 3.4 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-8}$</tex>(<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex>0.1)dyr<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>. This continuous period increase may be caused by mass transfer from the secondary component to the primary one on a thermal timescale, which is consistent with the Algol-like semi-detached configuration of EG Cep. Combining with the spectroscopic and photometric results, we derived a conservative mass-transfer rate of this target, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$dM/dt$</tex>= 3.0(<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex>0.1) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-8}M_{\odot}$</tex>yr<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>. The oscillation part of the period variation may be the result of a light-time effect due to the existence of a coplanar additional body with a mass of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_{3}$</tex>= 0.11<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_{\odot}$</tex>, and a corresponding radius of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$a_{3}$</tex>= 14AU. The presumed third body may play an important role in the evolution of this system.

articleTitle: A Galactic Center 50-kms$^{-1}$ Molecular Cloud with an Expanding Shell
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We performed high-resolution observations of a Galactic Center 50-km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex> molecular cloud in the CS <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J$</tex>= 1–0 line using the Nobeyama Millimeter Array (NMA). The molecular cloud mainly has three different spatial components with large velocity widths of up to 60 kms<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>. The northwest component is located at an apparent contact point to the Sgr A east shell, and elongated along the boundary of the shell. The large velocity width of the component is responsible for interaction with the Sgr A east shell. The molecular gas distribution in CS line emission is dissimilar to that observed previously in NH<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_3$</tex> line emissions. The appearance shows presumably the area of CS line emission enhanced by shock. The central and southwest components are located just out of the Sgr A east shell and far from it, respectively. However, these components have large velocity widths. We found a well-shaped circular molecular shell with expanding motion in the 50-km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex> molecular cloud. This is responsible for the large velocity width. The continuum source in the expanding molecular shell has a steep spectrum in mm-wavelengths, although this was not identified in a previous 5-GHz map. This source may be an SNR with an ionized sheath. From the aspect ratio of an expanding molecular shell of 1.1, the magnetic field in/around the shell is estimated to be smaller than 100<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu$</tex>Gauss. This weak magnetic field is consistent with on-going active star formation in the 50-km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex> molecular cloud. A comparison among CS line emission, low-frequency continuum, and millimeter continuum toward the 50-km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex> molecular cloud suggests a face-on view of the Sgr A region. The molecular cloud is located in the Sgr A halo region.

articleTitle: A Photometric Study of the Near-Contact Binary WY Tauri
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: CCD photometric observations for the eclipsing binary WY Tauri are firstly presented. Three new minimum timings in 2006 and 2008 have been determined. Using Wilson–Devinney binary code, the photometric solution was simultaneously deduced from <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$VR$</tex> light curves. Photometric results indicate that WY Tau is a semi-detached binary, whose secondary component fills its Roche lobe. The mass ratio and orbital inclination are <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$q$</tex>= 0.508(<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex>0.006) and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$i$</tex>= 78<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\circ}$</tex>0(<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex>0<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\circ}$</tex>05), respectively. The filling factor of the primary component is 84.9%, indicating that this star is a near-contact binary. Based on all available eclipse timings since 1930, it is found that the (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$O-C$</tex>) curve may be described by either a long-term period increase or a cyclic variation. The continuous period increase at a rate of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$dP/dt$</tex>=+4.65 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-8} $</tex>d yr<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex> may be attributed to mass transferring from the secondary to the primary, identified by the semidetached configuration. With mass transferring, WY Tau may evolve into a contact binary.

articleTitle: Another Abundance Inhomogeneity in the South East Limb of the Cygnus Loop
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We observed the south east (SE) limb of the Cygnus Loop with Suzaku. Our spatially-resolved spectroscopic study shows that a one-<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$kT_\mathrm{e}$</tex> non-equilibrium ionization model represents our spectra fairly well. We find that the metal abundances obtained are all depleted relative to the solar values with a positional dependence along the radial direction of the Cygnus Loop. The abundances in the very edge of the limb show about half the solar value, whereas other regions inside the Loop show about 0.2-times the solar value, which has been believed to be a typical value for the Cygnus Loop limb. The “enhanced” abundance in the very edge of the SE limb is quite similar to that found in the north-east (NE) limb of the Loop, and thus this is another evidence of an abundance inhomogeneity in the limb regions of the Loop. The radio map shows a quite different feature: the NE limb is in the radio bright region, while the SE limb shows almost no radio. Therefore, the metal abundance variation in the SE limb can not be attributed to non-thermal emission. The abundance inhomogeneity as well as the metal depletion down to 0.2 times the solar value still remain an open question.

articleTitle: X-Ray Studies of HESS J1837-069 with Suzaku and ASCA: a VHE Gamma-Ray Source Originated from the Pulsar Wind Nebula
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present ASCA and Suzaku studies of the TeV source HESS J1837-069, which has not been identified in other wavelengths. We confirm the presence of two X-ray sources in the Suzaku XIS image, AX J1838.0-0655 and AX J1837.3-0652, near both ends of the elongated TeV emission region. The XIS spectra of the two sources were reproduced by an absorbed power-law model, whose parameters are all consistent with those determined by the ASCA data. Recently, 70.5 ms X-ray pulsation has been detected with RXTE in the sky region including HESS J1837-069 (Gotthelf & Halpern 2008, ApJ, 681, 515). Using the ASCA GIS data, which has both timing and imaging capabilities, we identified the pulsation source as AX J1838.0-0655. The pulse periods determined by ASCA and Suzaku, and that reported with RXTE indicate steady spin-down at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\dot{P}$</tex>= 4.917(4)<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex>10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-14}$</tex>s s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>. These results suggest that AX J1838.0-0655 is an intrinsically stable source, and presumably a pulsar wind nebula (PWN). We discuss the possibility that AX J1838.0-0655 is associated with HESS J1837-069 and the VHE <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\gamma$</tex>-ray emission is originated from the PWN.

articleTitle: Particle Propagation in the Galactic Center and Spatial Distribution of Non-Thermal X-Rays
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We showed that if the non-thermal emission from the galactic center in the range 14–40 keV is due to inverse bremsstrahlung emission of subrelativistic protons, their interactions with hot and cold fractions of the interstellar medium are equally important. Our estimation shows that about 30% of the total non-thermal flux from the GC in the range 14–40 keV is generated in regions of cold gas while the rest is produced by proton interaction with hot plasma. From the spatial distribution of 6.7 keV iron line we concluded the spatial distribution of hot plasma is strongly non-uniform that should be taken into account in analysis of proton propagation in the GC. From the Suzaku data we got independent estimates for the diffusion coefficient of subrelativistic protons in the GC, which was in the range 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{26}$</tex>–10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{27} $</tex>cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{2} $</tex>s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>.

articleTitle: Thermally Driven Winds from Radiatively Inefficient Accretion Flows
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Radiatively inefficient accretion flows (RIAFs) are a common feature of low-luminosity accretion flows, including quiescent states of X-ray binaries and low-lunimosity active galactic nuclei. Thermally driven winds are expected from such hot accretion flows. By assuming that the flow has a self-similarity structure in the radial direction, we solved the vertical structure of the wind and accretion flows simultaneously and evaluated the mass loss rates by wind. We have found that the ratio of the outflow rate to the accretion rate is approximately unity for a viscosity parameter of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha $</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lesssim$</tex> 0.1, despite some uncertainties in the angular momentum and temperature distributions. That is, the accretion rate in the RIAFs is roughly proportional to the radius. Moreover, we elucidated the effect of cooling by wind on the underneath accretion flow, finding that this effect could be important for calculating the energy spectrum of the RIAF. Observational implications are briefly discussed in the context of Sgr A<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^\ast$</tex>.

articleTitle: An Orbital Period Investigation of the Semi-Detached Near-Contact Binary DD Monocerotis
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The variations of the orbital period of the near-contact binary system DD Monocerotis were analyzed based on three new CCD times of light minimum together with others compiled from the literature. The general trend of the (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$O-C$</tex>)<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_1$</tex> curve indicates a continuous period increase at a rate of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$dP/dt$</tex>=+1.40 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-7}$</tex>d yr<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>. Meanwhile, by using all available photoelectric and CCD data, a small-amplitude period oscillation (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$A$</tex>= 0.0039 d; <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$T=$</tex> 18.8 yr) was found to be superimposed on the period increase. The continuous period increase is explained by mass transfer from the less-massive component to the more-massive one (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$dM_{2}/dt$</tex>=+6.99 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-8}M_{\odot}$</tex>yr<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>), which is consistent with the semi-detached configuration of the binary with a lobe-filling secondary discovered by Qian et al. (1997, A&AS, 125, 475). We showed that the timescale of the period change is close to the thermal time scale of the secondary, suggesting that DD Monocerotis is undergoing a case A mass transfer. The small-amplitude period oscillation reveals the presence of an extremely cool stellar companion (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_3$</tex>sin<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${i^{\prime}}$</tex>= 0.13<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_{\odot}$</tex>) in the system. Accumulation of photoelectric and CCD data will discover small-amplitude cyclic changes in many close binary stars in the future.

articleTitle: Black-Hole Winds with a Variable Eddington Factor
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We solve one-dimentinal spherically symmetric, optically thick black-hole winds under general relativity with the help of a variable Eddington factor, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$f$</tex>(<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\tau$</tex>, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\beta$</tex>), where <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\tau$</tex> is the optical depth and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\beta$</tex> is the flow velocity normalized by the speed of light. Relativistic radiation hydrodynamics under the moment formalism has several complex problems, such as a closure relation. Conventional relativistic moment equations closed with the traditional Eddington approximation in the comoving frame have a singularity, beyond which the flow cannot be accelerated. In order to avoid such a pathological behavior inherent in the relativistic moment formalism, we use a variable Eddington factor that depends on the flow velocity as well as the optical depth, for the case of spherically symmetric flow. We find luminous winds that can be accelerated by radiation pressure from a close vicinity to a black hole up to nearly the speed of light in a general-relativistic gravitational field.

articleTitle: Search for Near-Infrared Pulsation of the Anomalous X-Ray Pulsar 4U 0142+61
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We have searched for pulsation of the anomalous X-ray pulsar (AXP) 4U 0142+61 in the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$K^\prime$</tex> band (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lambda_{\rm eff}$</tex>= 2.11<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu$</tex>m) using the fast-readout mode of Infrared Camera and Spectrograph (IRCS) at the Subaru 8.2 m telescope. We found no significant signal at the pulse frequency expected by the precise ephemeris based on an X-ray monitoring observation with RXTE. Nonetheless, we obtained the best upper limit of 17% (90% C.L.) for the root-mean-square pulse fraction in the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$K^\prime$</tex> band. Combined with the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$i^\prime$</tex> band pulsation (Dhillon et al. 2005, MNRAS, 363, 609), the slope of the pulsed component (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$F_\nu \propto \nu^\alpha$</tex> in units of Jy) was constrained to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$>$</tex>-0.87 (90% C.L.) for an interstellar extinction of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$A_{V}$</tex>= 3.5.

articleTitle: Origin of 6.4 keV Line Emission from Molecular Clouds in the Galactic Center
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We analyze the 6.4 keV line and continuum emission from the molecular cloud Sgr B2 and the source HESS J1745-303, which is supposed to be a complex of molecular gas. From the HESS results it follows that Sgr A<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^\ast$</tex> is a source of high energy protons, which penetrate into molecular clouds producing there a TeV gamma-ray flux. We present arguments that Sgr A<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^\ast$</tex> may also produce a flux of subrelativistic protons which generate the 6.4 keV line and bremsstrahlung continuum emission from the clouds.

articleTitle: Photometric Studies of a WZ Sge-Type Dwarf Nova Candidate, ASAS 160048-4846.2
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We report on our time-resolved CCD photometry during the 2005 June superoutburst of a WZ Sge-type dwarf nova candidate, ASAS 160048-4846.2. The ordinary superhumps of the object underwent a complex evolution during the superoutburst. The superhump amplitude experienced a regrowth and had two peaks. The superhump period decreased when the superhump amplitude reached the first maximum, subsequently increased gradually until the second maximum of the amplitude, and finally decreased again. Investigating other SU UMa-type dwarf novae, which show an increase in superhump period, we found the same trend of the superhump evolution in superoutbursts of them. We speculate that the superhump regrowth in the amplitude has a direct relation to the increase in superhump period, and all SU UMa-type dwarf novae with a superhump regrowth follow the same evolution of the ordinary superhumps as that of ASAS 160048-4846.2.

articleTitle: GreeM: Massively Parallel TreePM Code for Large Cosmological N-body Simulations
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: In this paper, we describe the implementation and performance of GreeM, a massively parallel TreePM code for large-scale cosmological N-body simulations. GreeM uses a recursive multi-section algorithm for domain decomposition. The size of the domains are adjusted so that the total calculation time of the force becomes the same for all processes. The loss of performance due to non-optimal load balancing is around 4%, even for more than 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^3$</tex> CPU cores. GreeM runs efficiently on PC clusters and massively-parallel computers, such as a Cray XT4. The measured calculation speed on Cray XT4 is 5 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^4$</tex> particles per second per CPU core, for the case of an opening angle of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\theta$</tex>= 0.5, if the number of particles per CPU core is larger than 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^6$</tex>.

articleTitle: The Atacama Compact Array (ACA)
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: For realizing high fidelity of imaging with mosaicing observations, the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) consists of a homogeneous array of 12 m antennas (12 m Array) and the Atacama Compact Array (ACA) in order to cover all spatial frequency Fourier components of the brightness distribution of observed sources. The array is located at an altitude site of about 5000 m with an operating wavelength range of 0.3 to 3 mm. ACA is an array composed of four 12 m dishes [TP (Total Power) Array] and twelve 7 m dishes (7 m Array). The 7 m Array has a very compact configuration to take short-baseline data corresponding to the low spatial frequency Fourier components. The 7 m Array has two configurations extended over 30-50 m to avoid shadowing at low elevation. The scientific importances and operation concepts of ACA, and the system design of ACA and its performance are presented in this paper.

articleTitle: The MAXI Mission on the ISS: Science and Instruments for Monitoring All-Sky X-Ray Images
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The Monitor of All-sky X-ray Image (MAXI) mission is the first astronomical payload to be installed on the Japanese Experiment Module — Exposed Facility (JEM-EF or Kibo-EF) on the International Space Station. It has two types of X-ray slit cameras with wide FOVs and two kinds of X-ray detectors consisting of gas proportional counters covering the energy range of 2 to 30 keV and X-ray CCDs covering the energy range of 0.5 to 12 keV. MAXI will be more powerful than any previous X-ray All Sky Monitor payloads, being able to monitor hundreds of Active Galactic Nuclei. A realistic simulation under optimal observation conditions suggests that MAXI will provide all-sky images of X-ray sources of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex>20 mCrab (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex>7 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-10} $</tex>erg cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-2} $</tex>s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex> in the energy band of 2–30 keV) from observations during one ISS orbit (90 min), <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex>4.5 mCrab for one day, and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex>2 mCrab for one week. The final detectability of MAXI could be <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex>0.2 mCrab for two years, which is comparable to the source confusion limit of the MAXI field of view (FOV). The MAXI objectives are: (1) to alert the community to X-ray novae and transient X-ray sources, (2) to monitor long-term variabilities of X-ray sources, (3) to stimulate multi-wavelength observations of variable objects, (4) to create unbiased X-ray source cataloges, and (5) to observe diffuse cosmic X-ray emissions, especially with better energy resolution for soft X-rays down to 0.5 keV.

articleTitle: Modeling and Reproducibility of Suzaku HXD PIN/GSO Background
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Suzaku Hard X-ray Detector (HXD) achieved the lowest background level than any other previously or currently operational missions sensitive in the energy range of 10–600 keV, by utilizing PIN photodiodes and GSO scintillators mounted in BGO active shields to reject particle background and Compton-scattered events as much as possible. Because it does not have an imaging capability nor rocking mode for the background monitor, the sensitivity is limited by the reproducibility of the non X-ray background (NXB) model. We modeled the HXD NXB, which varies with time as well as other satellites with a low-Earth orbit, by utilizing several parameters, including particle monitor counts and satellite orbital/attitude information. The model background is supplied as an event file in which the background events are generated by random numbers, and can be analyzed in the same way as the real data. The reproducibility of the NXB model depends on the event selection criteria (such as cut-off rigidity and energy band) and the integration time, and the 1<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sigma$</tex> systematic error is estimated to be less than 3% (PIN 15–40 keV) and 1% (GSO 50–100 keV) for more than 10 ks exposure.

articleTitle: Spectral Variation of the Seyfert 1 Galaxy MCG –6–30–15 Observed with Suzaku
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We have investigated the spectral variation of the Seyfert 1 galaxy MCG -6–30–15 observed with Suzaku in 2006 January for three separate periods spreading over fourteen days. We found that the time-averaged continuum energy spectrum between 1 keV and 40 keV can be approximated with a spectral model composed of a direct power-law component, its reflection component, two warm absorbers with different ionization states, and neutral absorption. We have taken two approaches to study its spectral variation at various timescales. The first approach was to make intensity-sliced spectra, and to study any correlation between the intensity and the spectral shape. The second approach was to study spectral changes between the intervals when the source flux is above (“bright state”) and below (“faint state”) the average for fixed time-intervals. In both approaches, we found a clear correlation between the intensity in the 6–10 keV band and the spectral ratio of 0.5–3.0 keV/6.0–10 keV. Such a spectral variation requires a change of the apparent slope of the direct component, whereas the shape and intensity of the reflection component are invariable. The observed apparent spectral change is explained by the variation of the ionization degree of one of the two warm absorbers due to the intrinsic source luminosity variation. The current results suggest that the warm absorber has a critical role to explain the observed continuum spectral shape and the variation of MCG -6–30–15, which is essential to constrain the parameters of the putatively broadened iron line emission feature.

articleTitle: Subaru Weak-Lensing Survey II: Multi-Object Spectroscopy and Cluster Masses
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present the first results of a multi-object spectroscopic campaign to follow up cluster candidates located via weak lensing. Our main goals are to search for spatial concentrations of galaxies that are plausible optical counterparts of the weak-lensing signals, and to determine the cluster redshifts from those of member galaxies. Around each of 36 targeted cluster candidates, we obtained 15–32 galaxy redshifts. For 28 of these targets, we confirmed a secure cluster identification, with more than five spectroscopic galaxies within a velocity of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex>3000 kms<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>. This includes three cases where two clusters at different redshifts are projected along the same line-of-sight. In 6 of the 8 unconfirmed targets, we found multiple small galaxy concentrations at different redshifts, each containing at least three spectroscopic galaxies. The weak-lensing signal around those systems was thus probably created by the projection of groups or small clusters along the same line-of-sight. In both of the remaining two targets, a single small galaxy concentration was found. In some candidate super-cluster systems, we found additional evidence of filaments connecting the main density peak to an additional nearby structure. For a subsample of our most cleanly measured clusters, we investigated the statistical relation between their weak-lensing mass (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_{\rm NFW}$</tex>, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sigma_{\rm SIS}$</tex>) and the velocity dispersion of their member galaxies (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sigma_{v}$</tex>), comparing our sample with optically and X-ray selected samples from the literature. Our lensing-selected clusters are consistent with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sigma_v$</tex>=<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sigma_{\rm SIS}$</tex>, with a similar scatter to that of optically and X-ray selected clusters. We also derived an empirical relation between the cluster mass and the galaxy velocity dispersion, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_{200}E$</tex>(<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z$</tex>) = 11.0 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{14}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sigma_v/$</tex>1000 kms<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>)<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{3.0}h^{-1}M_\odot$</tex>, which is in reasonable agreement with predictions of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$N$</tex>-body simulations in the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Lambda$</tex>CDM cosmology.

articleTitle: Suzaku Observations of Abell 1795: Cluster Emission to r200
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We report Suzaku observations of the galaxy cluster Abell 1795 that extend to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$r_{200}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\approx$</tex> 2 Mpc, the radius within which the mean cluster mass density is 200 times the cosmic critical density. These observations are the first to probe the state of the intracluster medium in this object at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$r$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$>$</tex> 1.3 Mpc. We sample two disjoint sectors in the cluster outskirts (1.3 Mpc <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$<$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$r$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$<$</tex> 1.9 Mpc) and detect X-ray emission in only one of them to a limiting (3<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sigma$</tex>) soft X-ray surface brightness of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$B_{0.5{\rm }2 {\rm keV}}$</tex>= 1.8 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-12} $</tex>erg s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1} $</tex>cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-2} $</tex>deg<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-2} $</tex>, a level less than 20% of the cosmic X-ray background brightness. We trace the run of temperature with radius at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$r$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$>$</tex> 0.4 Mpc and find that it falls relatively rapidly (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$T_{{\rm deprojected}}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\propto$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$r^{-0.9}$</tex>), reaching a value about one third of its peak at the largest radius we can measure it. Assuming the intracluster medium is in hydrostatic equilibrium and is polytropic, we find a polytropic index of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Gamma$</tex>= 1.3<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{+0.3}_{-0.2}$</tex> and we estimate a mass of (4.1<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{+0.5}_{-0.3}$</tex>) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{14} M_{\odot}$</tex> within 1.3 Mpc, somewhat (2.7<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sigma$</tex>) lower than that reported by previous observers. However, our observations provide evidence for departure from hydrostatic equilibrium at radii as small as <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$r$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex> 1.3 Mpc <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\approx r_{500}$</tex> in this apparently regular and symmetrical cluster.

articleTitle: A Large-Scale 13CO Mapping of the W 49 A Molecular Cloud Complex
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{13}$</tex>CO (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J$</tex>= 1-0) and C<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{18}$</tex>O (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J$</tex>= 1-0) maps of the W 49 A molecular cloud complex observed at a resolution of 17<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$''$</tex> (HPBW). Fourteen features (MHH-1 to MHH-14) were identified in the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{13}$</tex>CO velocity channel maps, most of them distributed within an area of 6<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$'$</tex> (20 pc) in diameter with their total mass amounting to 1.7 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{6}M_\odot$</tex>. The features have a three-dimensional velocity dispersion of 8 km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>, which leads to a mean free time per feature of 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{6}$</tex>yr. This suggests that they are interacting one another in a region of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>20 pc in diameter. The feature MHH-1, which corresponds to W 49 N, is unique in that it exhibits a large velocity width (15 km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex> FWHM) and is compact in size (2.3 pc <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 3.0 pc FWHM), while containing a large mass of 2.4 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{5}M_\odot$</tex>. This indicates that the free-fall time of MHH-1 is on the order of 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{5}$</tex>yr, an order of magnitude smaller than that of the entire complex. It has turned out that MHH-1 has a smaller spatial width at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$V_{\rm LSR}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lesssim$</tex> 8 km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex> than at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$>rsim$</tex>8 km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>. This result, together with the line-profile characteristics of various optically thin lines, suggests that at least two massive clouds with different radial velocities exist toward MHH-1. The massive compact feature may have been produced by the interaction of the two different velocity clouds.

articleTitle: Hard X-Ray Properties of the Merging Cluster Abell 3667 as Observed with Suzaku
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Wide-band Suzaku data on the merging cluster Abell 3667 were examined for hard X-ray emission in excess to the known thermal component. Suzaku detected X-ray signals in a wide energy band from 0.5 to 40 keV. The hard X-ray (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$>$</tex>10 keV) flux observed by the HXD around the cluster center cannot be explained by a simple extension of the thermal emission with an average temperature of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>7 keV. The emission is most likely to be from a very hot (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$kT$</tex> <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$>$</tex> 13.2 keV) thermal component around the cluster center, produced via a strong heating process in a merger. In the north-west radio relic, no signature of non-thermal emission was observed. Using the HXD, the overall upper-limit flux within a 34<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^\prime$</tex> <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 34<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^\prime$</tex> field-of-view around the relic was derived to be 5.3 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-12}$</tex>ergs<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-2}$</tex> in the 10–40 keV band, after subtracting the ICM contribution estimated using the XIS or the XMM-Newton spectra. Directly on the relic region, the upper limit is further tightened by the XIS data to be less than 7.3 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-13}$</tex>ergs<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-2}$</tex>, when converted into the 10–40 keV band. The latter value suggest that the average magnetic field within the relic is higher than 1.6 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu$</tex>G. The non-thermal pressure due to magnetic fields and relativistic electrons may be as large as <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>20% of the thermal pressure in the region.

articleTitle: Energy Spectra of the Soft X-Ray Diffuse Emission in Fourteen Fields Observed with Suzaku
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The soft diffuse X-ray emission of twelve fields observed with Suzaku are presented together with two additional fields from previous analyses. All have galactic longitudes 65<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^\circ $</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$<$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ell$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$<$</tex> 295<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^\circ $</tex> to avoid contributions from the very bright diffuse source that extends at least 30<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^\circ $</tex> from the Galactic center. The surface brightnesses of the Suzaku nine fields for which apparently uncontaminated ROSAT All Sky Survey (RASS) were available were statistically consistent with the RASS values, with an upper limit for differences of 17 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-6}$</tex>cs<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>arcmin<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-2}$</tex> in R45-band. The OVII and OVIII intensities are well correlated to each other, and OVII emission shows an intensity floor at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>2 photonss<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-2}$</tex>str<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex> (LU). The high-latitude OVIII emission shows a tight correlation with excess of OVII emission above the floor, with (OVIII intensity) = 0.5 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> [(OVII intensity) - 2LU], suggesting that temperatures averaged over different line-of-sight show a narrow distribution around <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>0.2 keV. We consider that the offset intensity of OVII arises from the Heliospheric solar wind charge exchange and perhaps from the local hot bubble, and that the excess OVII (2–7LU) is emission from more distant parts of the Galaxy. The total bolometric luminosity of this galactic emission is estimated to be 4 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{39}$</tex>ergs<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>, and its characteristic temperature may be related to the virial temperature of the Galaxy.

articleTitle: High-Resolution Near-Infrared Images of the T Tauri Binary System XZ Tauri
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
