articleTitle: An X-Ray Face-On View of the Sagittarius B Molecular Clouds Observed with Suzaku
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present a new methodology to derive the positions of the Sagittarius (Sgr) B molecular clouds (MCs) along the line of sight, as an application study of the Galactic center diffuse X-rays (GCDX). The GCDX are composed of hot plasma emission of about 7 keV and 1 keV temperatures, and non-thermal continuum emission including the 6.4 keV line from neutral irons. The former, the Galactic center plasma emission (GCPE), is uniformly distributed over 1<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^\circ$</tex> in longitude, while the latter is clumpy emission produced by Thomson scattering and fluorescence from MCs irradiated by external X-rays (the X-ray reflection nebula emission: XRNE). We examined the Suzaku X-ray spectra of the GCPE and XRNE near to the Sgr B MC complex, and found that the spectra suffer from two different absorptions of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$N_{\rm H}$</tex> (Abs1) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\geq$</tex>10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{23}$</tex>H cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-2}$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$N_{\rm H}$</tex> (Abs2) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\simeq$</tex>6 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{22}$</tex>H cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-2}$</tex>. Abs1 is proportional to the 6.4 keV-line flux, and hence is due to the MCs, while Abs2 is typical of interstellar absorption toward the Galactic center. Assuming that the GCPE plasma is spherically-extended around Sgr A<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^\ast$</tex> with a uniform density and the same angular distribution of the two temperature components, we quantitatively estimated the line-of-sight positions of the MCs from the flux ratio the GCPE spectrum suffered by Abs1 and that with no Abs1. The results suggest that the Sgr B MCs are located at the near side of Sgr A<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^\ast$</tex> in the GCPE.

articleTitle: Design and In-Orbit Performance of the Suzaku Wide-Band All-Sky Monitor
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The Suzaku Wide-band All-sky Monitor (WAM) consists of thick BGO anti-coincidence shields of the Hard X-ray Detectors (HXD). It views about half of the sky and has a geometrical area of 800 cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^2$</tex> per sdide and an effective area of 400 cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^2$</tex>, even at 1 MeV. Hence, the WAM can provide unique opportunities to detect high-energy emission from GRBs and solar flares in the sub-MeV to MeV range. The WAM has detected more than 400 GRBs and 100 solar flares since its launch. This paper describes the in-flight performance of the HXD/WAM during the initial two years of operations, including the in-flight energy response, spectral and timing capabilities, and in-orbit background.

articleTitle: Force-Free Black Hole Magnetospheres
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: It is argued that a force-free degenerate electrodynamic (FFDE) magnetosphere of a Kerr black hole with 0 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$<$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Omega _{\rm F}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$<$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${\Omega_{\rm H}}$</tex> consists of the outer classical and inner general-relativistic domains. This is described by a simple DC dual-circuit model, with dissipative membranes as two loads at a “force-free infinity surface” (S<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_{{\rm ff}\infty }$</tex>) with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\omega$</tex>= 0 and at a “force-free horizon surface” (S<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_{\rm ffH}$</tex>) with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\omega$</tex>=<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${\Omega_{\rm H}}$</tex>, where <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\omega$</tex>, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${\Omega_{\rm H}}$</tex>, and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Omega _{\rm F}$</tex> are the frame-dragging, the horizon and the field line angular frequencies. It is beneath upper null surface, S<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_{\rm N}$</tex>, at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\omega$</tex>=<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Omega _{\rm F}$</tex> between the two domains that dual unipolar batteries (double EMF’s) exist back-to-back, oppositely directed, with a pair-creation gap between. The total energy flux <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${\boldsymbol{S}}_E$</tex> is a linear sum of the two fluxes: the hole’s outward spin-down energy flux <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${\boldsymbol{S}}_{\rm SD}$</tex> originating at S<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_{\rm ffH}$</tex> and the Poynting flux <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\boldsymbol{S}_{\rm EM}$</tex> emitted at S<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_{\rm N}$</tex> in both the outward and inward directions, with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${\boldsymbol{S}}_E$</tex> being proportional to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Omega _{\rm F}$</tex>, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${\boldsymbol{S}}_{\rm SD}$</tex> to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\omega$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\boldsymbol{S}_{\rm EM}$</tex> to (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Omega _{\rm F}$</tex>-<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\omega$</tex>) along each field line. Applying a perturbation method for a split-monopolar field with a spin-parameter <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$h$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ll$</tex> 1, the analytic solution of the stream equation is given, and the double eigenvalue problem due to the ‘criticality condition’ at the outer/inner fast surfaces S<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_{\rm oF}$</tex>/S<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_{\rm iF}$</tex> and the ‘boundary condition’ at S<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_{\rm N}$</tex> is solved to yield the final eigenvalue <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Omega _{\rm F}$</tex>, in terms of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${\Omega_{\rm H}}$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$f_{\rm H}$</tex>= 0.5676. The ratio of the output power reaching S<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_{{\rm ff}\infty }$</tex> to the dissipation on S<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_{\rm ffH}$</tex> is <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\epsilon$</tex>= 1 + (4/5)(1 -<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$f_{\rm H}$</tex>) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$h^2$</tex>.

articleTitle: Suzaku and Multi-Wavelength Observations of OJ 287 during the Periodic Optical Outburst in 2007
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Suzaku observations of the blazar OJ 287 were performed in 2007 April 10–13 and November 7–9. They correspond to a quiescent and a flaring state, respectively. The X-ray spectra of the source can be well-described with single power-law models in both exposures. The derived X-ray photon index and the flux density at 1 keV were found to be <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Gamma$</tex>= 1.65<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm $</tex>0.02 and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$S_{\rm 1 keV}$</tex>= 215<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm $</tex>5 nJy in the quiescent state. In the flaring state, the source exhibited a harder X-ray spectrum (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Gamma$</tex>= 1.50<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm $</tex>0.01) with a nearly doubled X-ray flux density of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$S_{\rm 1 keV}$</tex>= 404<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{+6}_{-5} $</tex>nJy. Moreover, significant hard X-ray signals were detected up to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex>27 keV. In cooperation with Suzaku, simultaneous radio, optical, and very-high-energy <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\gamma $</tex>-ray observations of OJ 287 were performed with the Nobeyama Millimeter Array, the KANATA telescope, and the MAGIC telescope, respectively. The radio and optical fluxes in the flaring state (3.04<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm $</tex>0.46 Jy and 8.93<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm $</tex>0.05 mJy at 86.75 Hz and in the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$V$</tex>-band, respectively) were found to be higher by a factor of 2–3 than those in the quiescent state (1.73<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm $</tex>0.26 Jy and 3.03<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm $</tex>0.01 mJy at 86.75 Hz and in the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$V$</tex>-band, respectively). No notable <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\gamma $</tex>-ray events were detected in either observation. The spectral energy distribution of OJ 287 indicated that the X-ray spectrum was dominated by inverse Compton radiation in both observations, while synchrotron radiation exhibited a spectral cutoff at around the optical frequency. Furthermore, no significant difference in the synchrotron cutoff frequency was found between the quiescent and flaring states. According to a simple synchrotron self-Compton model, the change of the spectral energy distribution is due to an increase in the energy density of electrons with small changes of both the magnetic field strength and the maximum Lorentz factor of electrons.

articleTitle: Unified Rotation Curve of the Galaxy — Decomposition into de Vaucouleurs Bulge, Disk, Dark Halo, and the 9-kpc Rotation Dip —
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present a unified rotation curve of the Galaxy re-constructed from existing data by re-calculating the distances and velocities for a set of Galactic constants, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$R_0$</tex>= 8 kpc and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$V_0$</tex>= 200 km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>. We decomposed it into a bulge with de Vaucouleurs-law profile of half-mass scale radius 0.5 kpc and mass 1.8 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{10}M_\odot$</tex>, an exponential disk of scale radius 3.5 kpc and 6.5 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{10}M_\odot$</tex>, and an isothermal dark halo of terminal velocity 200 km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>. A <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$r^{1/4}$</tex>-law fit was obtained for the first time for the Milky Way’s rotation curve. After fitting by these fundamental structures, two local minima, or dips, of the rotation velocity are prominent at radii 3 and 9 kpc. The 3-kpc dip is consistent with the observed bar. It is alternatively explained by a massive ring with the density maximum at a radius of 4 kpc. The 9-kpc dip is clearly exhibited as the most peculiar feature in the Galactic rotation curve. We explain it by a massive ring of amplitude as large as 0.3 to 0.4-times the disk density with the density peak at a radius of 11 kpc. This great ring may be related to the Perseus arm, while no peculiar feature of HI-gas is associated.

articleTitle: High-Dispersion Spectroscopic Study of Solar Twins: HIP 56948, HIP 79672, and HIP 100963
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: An intensive spectroscopic study was performed for three representative solar twins (HIP 56948, HIP 79672, and HIP 100963) as well as for the Sun (Moon; reference standard), with intentions of (1) quantitatively discussing the relative-to-Sun similarities based on the precisely established differential parameters and (2) investigating the reason that causes the Li abundance differences, despite their similarities. It was concluded that HIP 56948 most resembles the Sun in every respect, including the Li abundance (though not perfectly similar) among the three, and deserves the name of “closest-ever solar twin”, while HIP 79672 and HIP 100963 have a somewhat higher effective temperature and appreciably higher surface Li composition. While there is an indication of Li being rotation-dependent, because the projected rotation in HIP 56948 (and the Sun) is slightly lower than the other two, the rotational difference alone does not seem to be so large as to efficiently produce a marked change in Li. Rather, this may be more likely to be attributed (at least partly) to a slight difference in <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$T_{\rm eff}$</tex> via some <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$T_{\rm eff}$</tex>-sensitive Li-controlling mechanism. Since the abundance of Be was found to be essentially solar for all stars irrespective of Li, any physical process causing the Li diversity should work only on Li without affecting Be.

articleTitle: New Spectral State of Supercritical Accretion Flow with Comptonizing Outflow
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Supercritical accretion flows inevitably produce radiation-pressure driven outflows, which Compton up-scatter soft photons from the underlying accretion flow, thereby making hard emission. We performed two-dimensional radiation hydrodynamic simulations of supercritical accretion flows and outflows, while incorporating such Compton scattering effects, and demonstrated that there appears a new hard spectral state at higher photon luminosities than that of the slim-disk state. In this state, as the photon luminosity increases, the photon index decreases and the fraction of the hard emission increases. The Compton <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$y$</tex>-parameter is on the order of unity (and thus the photon index will be <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>2) when the apparent photon luminosity is <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${\sim}$</tex> 30<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L_{\rm E}$</tex> (with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L_{\rm E}$</tex> being the Eddington luminosity) for nearly face-on sources. This explains the observed spectral hardening of the ULX NGC 1313 X-2 in its brightening phase, and thus supports the model of supercritical accretion onto stellar-mass black holes in this ULX.

articleTitle: Broad-Band Spectrum of the Black Hole Candidate IGR J17497-2821 Studied with Suzaku
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The broad-band 1–300 keV Suzaku spectrum of IGR J17497-2821, the X-ray transient discovered by INTEGRAL in 2006 September, is presented. Suzaku observed IGR J17497-2821 on September 25, eight days after its discovery, for a net exposure of about 53 ks. During the Suzaku observation, IGR J17497-2821 is very bright, 2 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{37}\>$</tex>erg s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex> at 8 kpc in the 1–300 keV range, and shows a hard spectrum, typical of black hole candidates in the low-hard state. Despite the multi-mission X-ray monitoring of the source, only with Suzaku is it possible to obtain a broad-band spectrum in the 1–300 keV range with a very high signal to noise ratio. A sum of a multi-color disc and a thermal Comptonization component with mild reflection is a good representation of our IGR J17497-2821 Suzaku spectrum. The spectral properties of the accretion disc as well as the cut-off energy in the spectrum at about 150 keV are clearly detected and constrained. We discuss the implications on the physical model used to interpret the data and the comparison with previous results.

articleTitle: Discovery of Molecular Loop 3 in the Galactic Center: Evidence for a Positive-Velocity Magnetically Floated Loop towards L= 355$^\circ$–359$^\circ$
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We have discovered a molecular dome-like feature towards 355<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\circ}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\leq$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$l$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\leq$</tex> 359<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\circ}$</tex> and 0<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\circ}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\leq$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$b$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\leq$</tex> 2<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\circ}$</tex>. The large velocity dispersions of 50–100 km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex> of this feature are much larger than those in the Galactic disk, and indicate that the feature is located in the Galactic center, probably within <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex>1 kpc of Sgr A<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\ast}$</tex>. The distribution has a projected length of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex>600 pc and a height of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex>300 pc from the Galactic disk, and shows a large-scale monotonic velocity gradient of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex>130 km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex> per <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex>600 pc. The feature is also associated with HI gas having a more continuous spatial and velocity distribution than that of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${}^{12}$</tex>CO. We interpret the feature as being a magnetically floated loop similar to loops 1 and 2, and name it “loop 3”. Loop 3 is similar to loops 1 and 2 in its height and length, but is different from loops 1 and 2 in that the inner part of loop 3 is filled with molecular emission. We have identified two foot points at both ends of loop 3. HI, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${}^{12}$</tex>CO, and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${}^{13}$</tex>CO datasets were used to estimate the total mass and the kinetic energy of loop 3 to be <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex>3.0 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{6} M_\odot$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex>1.7 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{52} $</tex>erg. The huge size, velocity dispersions, and energy are consistent with the magnetic origin of the Parker instability, as in the case of loops 1 and 2, but is difficult to be explained by multiple stellar explosions. We argue that loop 3 is in an earlier evolutionary phase than loops 1 and 2 based on the inner-filled morphology and the relative weakness of the foot points. This discovery indicates that the western part of the nuclear gas disk of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex>1 kpc radius is dominated by the three well-developed magnetically floated loops, and suggests that the dynamics of the nuclear gas disk is strongly affected by magnetic instabilities.

articleTitle: Diffuse 18  $\mu$m Emission around TYC 3159-6-1 Discovered by the AKARI MIR All-Sky Survey
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We report on observations of the mysterious object TYC 3159-6-1 located toward the Cygnus X region. It shows interesting characteristics in the AKARI mid-infrared All-Sky Survey. The central star is clearly detected as a point source at 9 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu$</tex>m, while no point-like source, but a large shell-like structure is seen around the source at 18 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu$</tex>m. The optical spectrum indicates the presence of the weak H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex>emission on the red smooth continuum, whereas the mid-infrared <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$N$</tex>band spectrum shows neither excess emission nor significant silicate absorption. Interferometric continuum observations at 104 GHz do not show any appreciable peak at the position of the star. On the basis of these observations, we investigate three possibilities of concerning the nature of TYC 3159-6-1: a nearby young stellar object, a heavily extincted high-mass star, and an asymptotic giant branch (AGB) star with a detached shell. We conclude that none of these cases can account for the observations consistently, and the nature of TYC 3159-6-1 remains a mystery.

articleTitle: AKARI Far-Infrared Spectroscopic Observations of the Galactic Center Region
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We have observed the Quintuplet- and Arches-cluster regions with the Fourier Transform Spectrometer (FTS) of the Far-Infrared Surveyor (FIS) aboard AKARI to investigate the physical conditions of interstellar matter around the clusters. The FIS-FTS mapping data reveal differences in the spatial distribution among the far-infrared [O III], [N II], and [C II] line emissions near the Arches cluster; the emission of an ionic line with a higher ionization potential is distributed closer to the Arches cluster. This clearly indicates that UV photons from the Arches cluster are ionizing the surface of nearby molecular clouds, and penetrating deeper to dissociate the cloud. We have estimated the effective temperature of the Arches cluster to be about 34000 K from the ratio of the [O III]/[N II] lines.

articleTitle: Modified Slim-Disk Model Based on Radiation-Hydrodynamic Simulation Data: The Conflict between Outflow and Photon Trapping
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Photon trapping and outflow are two key physics issues associated with supercritical accretion flow. We investigated the conflict between these two processes based on two-dimensional radiation-hydrodynamic (RHD) simulation data, and constructed a simplified (radially) one-dimensional model. Mass loss due to outflow, which is not considered in the slim-disk model, reduces the surface density of the flow, and if very significantly, it can totally suppress the photon-trapping effects. If photon trapping is very significant, conversely, outflow can be suppressed because the radiation-pressure force is reduced. To see what actually occurs, we examined the RHD simulation data and evaluated the accretion and outflow rates as functions of the radius. We have found that the accretion rate monotonically decreases, while the outflow rate increases, as the radius decreases. However, the accretion remains constant at small radii, inside several Schwarzschild radii, since the outflow is suppressed by photon trapping effects. To understand the conflict between the photon trapping and outflow in a simpler way, we modeled the radial distribution of the accretion rate from our simulation data, and built up a new (radially) one-dimensional model, which is similar to the slim-disk model, but incorporates mass loss effects due to the outflow. We find that the surface density (and, hence, the optical depth) is greatly reduced even inside the trapping radius, compared to the case without outflow, whereas the effective temperature distribution hardly changes. That is, the emergent spectra do not sensitively depend on the amount of mass outflow. We conclude that the slim-disk approach is valid for interpreting observations, even if the outflow is taken into account. The observational implications of our findings are briefly discussed in relation to ultra-luminous X-ray sources.

articleTitle: Suzaku Observation of the Metallicity Distribution in the Elliptical Galaxy NGC 4636
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: NGC 4636, an X-ray bright elliptical galaxy, was observed for 70 ks with Suzaku. Thanks to low background and good energy resolution of the XIS, we succeeded to estimate the foreground Galactic emission accurately, and, for the first time, measure the metal abundance distributions out to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex>28<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${}^\prime$</tex> (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\simeq $</tex>140 kpc) for O, Mg, Si, and Fe. The metal abundances are as high as <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$>$</tex>1 solar within 4<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${}^\prime$</tex>, and decreases by <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex>50% from the center toward the outer region. In addition, the O to Fe abundance ratio is about 0.6<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex>1.0 solar in all analyzed regions, indicating that metal products by SNe II and SNe Ia have mixed and diffused to the outer region of the galaxy. Furthermore, comparing the O and Fe mass distributions with those of NGC 1399, we found the metal mass-to-light ratio (MLR) of NGC 4636 to be 2–3 times larger. Therefore, the metal distributions in NGC 4636 are less extended than those in NGC 1399, possibly due to environmental factors, such as frequency of galaxy interaction. We also found that MLRs of NGC 4636 at 0.1<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ r_{180}$</tex> are <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex>5-times smaller than those of clusters of galaxies, possibly consistent with the correlation between temperature and MLR of other spherically symmetric groups of galaxies. We also confirmed a signature of the resonance scattering of the Fe XVII line in the central region, as reported based on the XMM-Newton RGS observation.

articleTitle: A Massive Substellar Companion to the Massive Giant HD 119445
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We detected a brown dwarf-mass companion around the intermediate-mass giant star HD 119445 (G6III) using the Doppler technique. This discovery is the first result from a Korean-Japanese planet search program based on precise radial velocity measurements. The radial velocity of this star exhibits a periodic Keplerian variation with a period, semiamplitude, and eccentricity of 410.2 d, 413.5 ms<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>, and 0.082, respectively. Adopting a stellar mass of 3.9<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_{\odot}$</tex>, we were able to confirm the presence of a massive substellar companion with a semimajor axis of 1.71AU and a minimum mass of 37.6<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_{\mathrm{J}}$</tex>, which falls in the middle of the brown dwarf-mass region. This substellar companion is the most massive ever discovered within 3AU of a central intermediate-mass star. The host star also ranks among the most massive stars with substellar companions ever detected by the Doppler technique. This result supports the current view of substellar systems that more massive substellar companions tend to exist around more massive stars, and may further constrain substellar system formation mechanisms.

articleTitle: Suzaku and XMM-Newton Observations of Diffuse X-Ray Emission from the Eastern Tip Region of the Carina Nebula
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The eastern tip region of the Carina Nebula was observed with the Suzaku XIS for 77 ks to conduct a high-precision spectral study of extended X-ray emission. XMM-Newton EPIC data of this region were also utilized to detect point sources. The XIS detected strong extended X-ray emission from the entire field-of-view with a 0.2–5 keV flux of 0.7–4<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex>10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-14}$</tex>ergs<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>arcmin<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-2}$</tex>. The emission has a blob-like structure that coincides with an ionized gas filament observed in mid-infrared images. Contributions of astrophysical backgrounds and the detected point sources were insignificant. Thus the emission is diffuse in nature. The X-ray spectrum of the diffuse emission was represented by a two-temperature plasma model with temperatures of 0.3 and 0.6 keV and an absorption column density of 2<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex>10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{21}$</tex>cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>. The X-ray emission showed normal nitrogen-to-oxygen abundance ratios and a high iron-to-oxygen abundance ratio. The spectrally deduced parameters, such as temperatures and column densities, are common to the diffuse X-ray emission near <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\eta$</tex> Car. Thus, the diffuse X-ray emission in these two fields may have the same origin. The spectral fitting results are discussed to constrain the origin in the context of stellar winds and supernovae.

articleTitle: Suzaku Observations of Tycho’s Supernova Remnant
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Tycho’s supernova remnant was observed by the XIS and HXD instruments onboard the Suzaku satellite on 2006 June 26–29 for 92 ks. The spectrum up to 30 keV was well fitted with a two-component model, consisting of a power-law with a photon index of 2.7 and a thermal bremsstrahlung model with a temperature of 4.7 keV. The former component can alternatively be modeled as synchrotron emission from a population of relativistic electrons with an estimated roll-off energy of around 1 keV. In the XIS spectra, in addition to the prominent Fe K<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex> line (6.445 keV), we observed for the first time significant K<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex> line emission from trace species Cr and Mn at energies of 5.48 keV and 5.95 keV, respectively. Faint K<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\beta$</tex> lines from Ca (4.56 keV) and Fe (7.11 keV) were also seen. The ionization states of Cr and Mn, based on their line centroids, are estimated to be similar to that of Fe K<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex> (FeXV or XVI).

articleTitle: Design of Corrective Beam Waveguide System for the ALMA/ACA 7-m Antenna
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: A beam waveguide system for connecting the ALMA front-end, which has been designed for the Cassegrain focus of the ALMA 12-m antenna, with the ALMA/ACA 7-m antenna was designed. The beam waveguide system, covering 30–950 GHz, consists of flat mirrors or prisms to modify the boresight tilt angle from the front-end, and recovers more than the half of the sensitivity loss caused by a misalignment between the front-end optics and the 7-m antenna. No mechanical alignment procedure is needed for installation of the beam waveguide system, and thus it does not impact on the maintenance/operation scheme of the front-end system. Beam-pattern measurements in the frequency ranges of ALMA bands 4 (144 GHz), 6 (252 GHz), and 8 (385 GHz) have confirmed that directions of the radiation patterns transmitted to the subreflector are successfully shifted by the beam waveguide system without any serious deformation of the beam. The aperture efficiencies calculated from the measured radiation patterns were determined to be 84.6% at 144 GHz, 86.1% at 252 GHz, and 84.8% at 385 GHz, which are consistent with those of a simulated radiation pattern.

articleTitle: The Origin of an Extended X-Ray Emission Apparently Associated with the Globular Cluster 47 Tucanae
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Using the Suzaku X-ray Imaging Spectrometer, we performed a 130 ks observation of an extended X-ray emission, which was shown by ROSAT and Chandra observations to apparently associate with the globular cluster 47 Tucanae. The obtained 0.5–6 keV spectrum was successfully fitted with a redshifted thin thermal plasma emission model whose temperature and redshift are 2.2<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{+0.2}_{-0.3} $</tex>keV (at the rest frame) and 0.34<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm $</tex>0.02, respectively. The derived parameters, including the temperature, redshift, and luminosity, indicate that the extended X-ray source is a background cluster of galaxies, and its projected location falls, by chance, on the direction of the proper motion of 47 Tucanae.

articleTitle: Suzaku Results on the Obscured Low-Luminosity Active Galactic Nucleus in NGC 4258
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: In 2006 June, the obscured low-luminosity active galactic nucleus in the nearby Seyfert 1.9 galaxy NGC 4258 was observed with Suzaku for <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>100 ks. Utilizing the XIS and the HXD, the nucleus emission was detected over a <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>2 to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>40 keV range, with an unabsorbed 2–10 keV luminosity of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>8 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{40}$</tex>ergs<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>; it varied by a factor of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>2 during the observation. Its 2–40 keV spectrum is reproduced by a single power law with a photon index of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Gamma$</tex> <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex> 2.0, absorbed by an equivalent hydrogen column of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>1.0 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{23}$</tex>cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^2$</tex>. The spectrum within <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$4{}^{\prime}$</tex> of the nucleus also required a softer thin-thermal emission, as well as an intermediate hardness component, attributable to integrated point sources. A weak neutral Fe-K<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex> florescence line was detected at an equivalent width of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>40 eV. A cold reflection component was not required by the data, with the reflector solid angle <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Omega$</tex> seen from the nucleus constrained as <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Omega /$</tex>2<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pi$</tex> <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lesssim$</tex> 0.3, assuming a general case of 60<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^\circ$</tex> inclination. The results suggest that the cold reflecting material around the nucleus is localized along our line of sight, rather than forming a thick torus.

articleTitle: Spectropolarimetry with the Hida Domeless Solar Telescope
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We developed a spectropolarimetry system with a ferroelectric liquid crystal polarization modulator for the 60-cm Domeless Solar Telescope of Hida Observatory. The telescope is equipped with two oblique-reflection mirrors, that alter the incident polarization before it reaches the polarimeter. Furthermore, it is impossible to calibrate the polarimeter using unpolarized light because of the instrumental polarization. Here, we develop a procedure to obtain the parameters of both the instrumental polarization and for the calibration of the polarimeter from the same calibration data sets. We apply the new procedure to carry out high-sensitivity spectropolarimetry. It is now possible to measure the polarizations of various photospheric and chromospheric lines with the Domeless Solar Telescope.

articleTitle: A Study of Combining Technique of Single-Dish and Interferometer Data: Imaging Simulations and Analysis
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We have investigated a technique of combining single-dish data and interferometer data in the spatial frequency domain, using imaging simulations and analytical considerations. Our study shows that there is an optimum of the relative weights between the visibility data of a single-dish and an interferometer. The quality of the reconstructed combined image achieves the highest values at relative weights where the mean of the difference between the synthesized beam and the CLEAN beam is close to zero. We also examined the (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$u$</tex>,<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$v$</tex>)-range that can be effectively used for the data combining by considering a blurring effect due to a pointing error. The error in single-dish deconvolution caused by the beam approximation is small with a large diameter of the single-dish aperture. The diameter should be at least 1.7-times larger than the minimum baseline of the interferometer for an amplitude accuracy better than 10%. Furthermore, we derived an estimate of the noise variance in the combined image, which agrees with our simulation results. The noise-added simulations demonstrate that there is a threshold of the noise level of the single-dish image, beyond which a large-scale error is emphasized in the combined image. We should take observation times to make at least the same noise level at the border of the spatial frequency between the single-dish and the interferometer. Although our examinations were assumed to use the 45 m telescope and NMA, our results concerning the required conditions for observations and data processes can be used in a general case of heterogeneous array imaging.

articleTitle: North Ecliptic Pole Wide Field Survey of AKARI: Survey Strategy and Data Characteristics
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present the survey strategy and the data characteristics of the North Ecliptic Pole (NEP) Wide Survey of AKARI. The survey was carried out for about one year starting from 2006 May with 9 passbands from 2.5 to 24 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu$</tex>m and the areal coverage of about 5.8 degree<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^2$</tex> centered on NEP. The survey depth reaches to 21.8 AB magnitude near infrared (NIR) bands, and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>18.6 AB magnitude at the mid infrared (MIR) bands such as 15 and 18 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu$</tex>m. The total number of sources detected in this survey is about 104000, with more sources in NIR than in the MIR. We have cross matched infrared sources with optically identified sources in CFHT imaging survey which covered about 2 degree<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^2$</tex> within NEP-Wide survey region in order to characterize the nature of infrared sources. The majority of the MIR sources at 15 and 18 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu$</tex>m bands are found to be star forming disk galaxies, with smaller fraction of early type galaxies and AGNs. We found that a large fraction (60%–80%) of bright sources in 9 and 11 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu$</tex>m is stars while stellar fraction decreases toward fainter sources. We present the histograms of the sources at MIR bands at 9, 11, 15, and 18 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu$</tex>m. The number of sources per magnitude thus varies as <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$m^{0.6}$</tex> for longer wavelength sources while shorter wavelength sources show steeper variation with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$m$</tex>, where <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$m$</tex> is the AB magnitude.

articleTitle: Suzaku Observation of Diffuse X-Ray Emission from the Open Cluster Westerlund 2: a Hypernova Remnant?
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present an analysis of Suzaku observations of the young open cluster Westerlund 2, which is filled with diffuse X-ray emission. We found that the emission consists of three thermal components, or two thermal and one non-thermal components. The upper limit of the energy flux of the non-thermal component is smaller than that in the TeV band observed with H.E.S.S. This may indicate that active particle acceleration has stopped in this cluster, and that the accelerated electrons have already cooled. The gamma-ray emission observed with H.E.S.S. is likely to come from high-energy protons, which hardly cool, in contrast with electrons. The metal abundances of the diffuse X-ray gas may indicate the explosion of a massive star in the past.

Author Keywords: Galaxy: open clusters and associations: individual (Westerlund 2)

articleTitle: The Nature of a Cosmic-Ray Accelerator, CTB 37 B, Observed with Suzaku and Chandra
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We report on Suzaku and Chandra observations of the young supernova remnant CTB 37 B, from which TeV <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\gamma$</tex>-rays were detected by the H.E.S.S. Cherenkov telescope. The 80 ks Suzaku observation provided us with a clear image of diffuse emission and high-quality spectra. The spectra revealed that the diffuse emission is comprised of thermal and non-thermal components. The thermal component can be represented by an NEI model with a temperature, a pre-shock electron density and an age of 0.9<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex>0.2 keV, 0.4<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex>0.1 cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-3}$</tex>, and 650<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{+2500}_{-300}$</tex>yr, respectively. This suggests that the explosion of CTB 37 B occurred in a low-density space. A non-thermal power-law component was found from the southern region of CTB 37 B. Its photon index of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>1.5 and a high roll-off energy (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$>rsim$</tex>15 keV) indicate efficient cosmic-ray acceleration. A comparison of this X-ray spectrum with the TeV <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\gamma$</tex>-ray spectrum leads us to conclude that the TeV <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\gamma$</tex>-ray emission seems to be powered by either multi-zone Inverse Compton scattering or the decay of neutral pions. The point source resolved by Chandra near the shell is probably associated with CTB 37 B, because of the common hydrogen column density with the diffuse thermal emission. Spectral and temporal characteristics suggest that this source is a new anomalous X-ray pulsar.

articleTitle: WD+MS Systems as Progenitors of Type Ia Supernovae with Different Metallicities
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The single-degenerate model for the progenitors of type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) is one of the two most popular models, in which a carbon–oxygen white dwarf accretes hydrogen-rich material from its companion, increases its mass to the Chandrasekhar mass limit, and then explodes as a SN Ia. Incorporating the prescription of Hachisu et al. (1999a, ApJ, 519, 314) for the accretion efficiency into Eggleton’s stellar evolution code and assuming that the prescription is valid for all metallicities, we carried out a detailed binary evolution study with different metallicities. We showed the initial and final parameter space for SNe Ia in a (log<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ P$</tex>–<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_{\rm 2}$</tex>) plane. The positions of some famous recurrent novae in the (log<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ P$</tex>–<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_{2}$</tex>) plane, as well as a supersoft X-ray source (SSS), RX J0513.9-6951 are well explained by our model, and our model can also explain the space velocity and mass of Tycho G, which is now suggested to be a companion star of Tycho’s supernova. Our study indicates that a SSS, V Sge, is a potential progenitor of supernovae, like SN 2002ic, if the delayed dynamical-instability model in Han and Podsiadlowski (2006, MNRAS, 368, 1095) is appropriate.

articleTitle: Implications of Bulk Velocity Structures in AGN Jets
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Synchrotron self-Compton (SSC) models and External Compton (EC) models of AGN jets with continually longitudinal and transverse bulk velocity structures have been constructed. The observed spectra show complex and interesting patterns in different velocity structures and viewing angles. These models were used to calculate the synchrotron and inverse Compton spectra of two typical BL Lac objects (BLO) (Mrk 421 and 0716+714) and (one) Flat Spectrum Radio Quasars (FSRQs) (3C 279), and to discuss the implications of jet bulk velocity structures in a unification of the BLO and FR I radio galaxies (FRI). By calculating the synchrotron spectra and SSC spectra of BL Lac object jets with continually bulk velocity structures, we have found that the spectra are much different from those in jets with a uniform velocity structure under increasing viewing angles. The unification of BLO and FRI is less constrained by the viewing angles, and would be imprinted by velocity structures intrinsic to the jets, themselves. By considering jets with bulk velocity structures constrained by the apparent speed, we discuss the velocity structures imprinted on the observed spectra for different viewing angles. We find that the spectra are greatly impacted by longitudinal velocity structures, because the volume elements are compressed or expanded. Finally, we present the EC spectra of FSRQs and FR II radio galaxies (FRII), and find that they are weakly affected by the velocity structures compared to synchrotron and SSC spectra.

articleTitle: Potassium Abundances in Red Giants of Mildly to Very Metal-Poor Globular Clusters
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: A non-LTE analysis of KI resonance lines at 7664.91 and 7698.97 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\AA$</tex> was carried out for 15 red giants belonging to three globular clusters of different metallicity (M 4, M 13, and M 15) along with two reference early-K giants (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\rho$</tex> Boo and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex> Boo), in order to check whether the K abundances are uniform within a cluster, and to investigate the behavior of the [K/Fe] ratio at the relevant metallicity range of -2.5 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lesssim$</tex> [Fe/H] <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lesssim$</tex>-1. We confirmed that [K/H] (as well as [Fe/H]) is almost homogeneous within each cluster to a precision of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lesssim$</tex> 0.1 dex, though dubiously large deviations are exceptionally seen for two peculiar stars showing signs of considerably increased turbulence in the upper atmosphere. The resulting [K/Fe] ratios are mildly supersolar by a few tenths of dex for three clusters, tending to gradually increase from <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex> 0.1–0.2 at [Fe/H] <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>-1 to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim+$</tex>0.3 at [Fe/H] <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>-2.5. This result connects reasonably well with the [K/Fe] trend of disk stars (-1 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lesssim$</tex> [Fe/H]) and that of extremely metal-poor stars (-4 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lesssim$</tex> [Fe/H] <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lesssim$</tex>-2.5). That is, [K/Fe] appears to continue a gradual increase from [Fe/H] <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex> 0 toward a lower metallicity regime down to [Fe/H] <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>-3, where a broad maximum of [K/Fe] <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>+0.3-0.4 is attained, possibly followed by a slight downturn at [Fe/H] <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lesssim$</tex>-3.

articleTitle: A New Mechanism for Massive Binary Black-Hole Evolution
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: It is still unknown how a binary black hole (BBH) evolves after its semi-major axis has reached the sub-parsec scale, where dynamical friction with neighboring stars is no longer effective (the so-called final-parsec problem). In this paper, we propose a new mechanism by which a massive BBH can naturally coalesce within a Hubble time. We consider the evolution of a BBH with a triple disk composed of an accretion disk around each black hole and one circumbinary disk surrounding them. While the circumbinary disk removes the orbital angular momentum of the BBH via a binary-disk resonant interaction, the mass transfer from the circumbinary disk to each black hole adds some fraction of its angular momentum to the orbital angular momentum of the BBH. We find that there is a critical value of the mass-transfer rate where extraction of the orbital angular momentum from the BBH is balanced with the addition of orbital angular momentum to the BBH. The semi-major axis of the BBH decays with time, whereas the orbital eccentricity of the BBH grows with time, if the mass-transfer rate is smaller than the critical one, and vice versa. Its evolutionary timescale is characterized by the product of the viscous timescale of the circumbinary disk and the ratio of the total black-hole mass to the mass of the circumbinary disk. Most massive BBHs are able to merge within a Hubble time by the proposed mechanism, which helps to solve the final parsec problem.

articleTitle: Uniting the Quiescent Emission and Burst Spectra of Magnetar Candidates
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Spectral studies of quiescent emission and bursts of magnetar candidates based on XMM-Newton, Chandra, and Swift data are presented. Spectra of both the quiescent emission and the burst for most magnetar candidates are reproduced by a photoelectrically absorbed two-blackbody function (2BB). There is a strong correlation between the lower and higher temperatures of 2BB (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$kT_{\mathrm{LT}}$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$kT_{\mathrm{HT}}$</tex>) for the magnetar candidates of which the spectra are well reproduced by 2BB. In addition, a square of radius for <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$kT_{\mathrm{LT}}$</tex> (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$R_{\mathrm{LT}}^2$</tex>) is well correlated with a square of radius for <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$kT_{\mathrm{HT}}$</tex> (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$R_{\mathrm{HT}}^2$</tex>). The ratio <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$kT_{\mathrm LT}/kT_{\mathrm HT}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\approx$</tex> 0.4 is nearly constant irrespective of the objects and/or emission types (i.e., the quiescent emission and the burst). This would imply that an emission mechanism is common among the magnetar candidates. The relation between the quiescent emission and the burst might be analogous to a relation between the solar microflare and the solar flare. Three anomalous X-ray pulsars (AXPs) (4U0142+614, 1RXSJ170849.0-400910, and 1E 2259+586) seem to have an excess above <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>7 keV, which well agrees with a nonthermal hard component discovered by the International Gamma-Ray Astrophysics Laboratory (INTEGRAL).
